title: CAN A PASTOR HAVE MULTIPLE WIVES AND GIRLFRIENDS?
paragraphs:
CAN A PASTOR HAVE MULTIPLE WIVES AND GIRLFRIENDS?
The Biblical Answer May Cost Someone Their Pulpit—But It Could Save a Church From Calling Scandal “Grace”
There is a question Christians sometimes whisper because answering it publicly can become uncomfortable very quickly:
Can a pastor have multiple wives and girlfriends and still remain a pastor?
Imagine the scene.
Sunday morning.
The worship has ended. The lights soften. A man walks toward the pulpit carrying a Bible.
People trust him.

A struggling husband listens because he wants to become a better man. A young woman takes notes because she believes this pastor will teach her what godly love looks like. A teenager watches because he is still deciding whether Christianity is real. A wounded wife sits quietly in the congregation asking God to restore her faith after betrayal nearly destroyed her.
Then something comes to light.
The pastor has another woman.
Maybe more than one.
Maybe someone calls them “girlfriends.”
Maybe there are secret messages, hidden meetings, sexual relationships, another household, or even claims that Scripture permits him to have multiple wives.
And suddenly the question changes.
It is no longer merely:
“Is my pastor a gifted preacher?”
It becomes:
“Does the Bible permit the man teaching us holiness to live this way?”
That question deserves something better than gossip.
Better than denominational politics.
Better than cultural tradition.
Better than outrage on social media.
It deserves Scripture.
And Scripture speaks with uncomfortable clarity.
When Paul describes the qualifications of an overseer in 1 Timothy 3:2, the Greek text contains this striking expression:
μιᾶς γυναικὸς ἄνδρα — mias gynaikos andra
Literally, the words are built around “one woman/wife” and “man/husband.”
Paul writes:
δεῖ οὖν τὸν ἐπίσκοπον ἀνεπίλημπτον εἶναι, μιᾶς γυναικὸς ἄνδρα…
The sense is:
“Therefore, the overseer must be above reproach, a husband/man of one wife/woman…”
The Greek matters.
μιᾶς — mias — means “one.”
γυναικός — gynaikos — can mean “woman” or “wife,” depending upon context.
ἀνήρ / ἄνδρα — anēr / andra — can mean “man” or “husband.”
Paul repeats essentially the same requirement when instructing Titus about appointing elders:
μιᾶς γυναικὸς ἀνήρ — mias gynaikos anēr.
Again:
A one-woman man.

This does not merely give us a mathematical formula for marital paperwork. The qualification sits inside a larger portrait of observable Christian character: above reproach, sober-minded, self-controlled, respectable, hospitable, able to teach, not violent, not controlled by money, and capable of governing his household faithfully.
The pastor is not being asked merely:
“How many marriage certificates do you possess?”
Scripture is asking:
“What kind of man are you when nobody is applauding?”
That distinction matters.

Scholars and Christian traditions have debated some applications of “husband of one wife”—including questions involving widowers who remarry, divorce and remarriage, and whether Paul’s expression specifically prohibits polygamy or more broadly describes marital and sexual faithfulness.
But none of those debates provides a loophole for a married pastor maintaining girlfriends or sexual partners outside his marriage.
None.
Because Scripture does not leave sexual faithfulness hanging on one disputed phrase.
Paul gives another remarkably symmetrical command in 1 Corinthians 7:2:
ἕκαστος τὴν ἑαυτοῦ γυναῖκα ἐχέτω, καὶ ἑκάστη τὸν ἴδιον ἄνδρα ἐχέτω.
In context, Paul is addressing πορνεία — porneia, sexual immorality.
Notice the symmetry.
Each man, his own wife.
Each woman, her own husband.
Not a pastor with a wife for church photographs and girlfriends for private pleasure.
Not holiness behind the microphone and secret sexuality behind a locked phone.
Not one covenant in daylight and another life after dark.

And before someone reaches into the Old Testament and says, “But David had multiple wives,” or, “Solomon had many wives,” we need to learn one of the most important principles of biblical interpretation:
The Bible recording something does not mean God is recommending it.
Scripture records murder.
That does not sanctify murder.
Scripture records deception.
That does not sanctify lying.
Scripture records adultery.
That does not turn adultery into discipleship.
And Scripture records polygamous households while repeatedly allowing us to see the jealousy, rivalry, fragmentation, favoritism, grief, and family disorder that so often followed.
If we want the clearest foundation for Christian marriage, we should not begin with fallen kings trying to satisfy fallen desires.
We should listen to Jesus.
Christ reaches behind human corruption and points back toward creation.
Genesis describes a man leaving father and mother, being joined to his wife, and the two becoming one flesh.
Jesus deliberately returns to that foundation when teaching about marriage.
Not:
“The powerful man accumulates women.”
But:
The two become one flesh.
This is where the issue becomes much deeper than denominational policy.
Marriage is covenant.
And Christian leadership is supposed to display a life increasingly surrendered to Christ.
A pastor is not sinless.
Please hear that carefully.
If churches required sinless pastors, every pulpit on earth would be empty.
Pastors need grace too.
Pastors can be tempted.
Pastors can fall.
Pastors can confess.
Pastors can repent.
Pastors can be forgiven.
And yes—
Jesus can restore a fallen pastor as a brother even when restoration to pastoral office is a separate question.
Those two things must never be confused.
Forgiveness does not automatically mean qualification.
Grace does not require pretending consequences disappeared.
Repentance does not mean a congregation must immediately return someone to authority.

A man may be completely forgiven by Christ while still needing to step away from pastoral leadership because Scripture places serious character requirements upon those entrusted with shepherding Christ’s people.
That is not cruelty.
That is taking both grace and shepherding seriously.
This is where churches sometimes make devastating mistakes.
They become so frightened of appearing judgmental that they rename compromise “grace.”
Or they become so furious about scandal that they forget the Gospel entirely.
Neither response is Christian.
Truth without grace can become a weapon.
Grace without truth becomes permission.
Jesus gives us neither counterfeit.
Jesus gives grace that tells the truth and truth that leads sinners toward grace.

So if a married pastor is secretly maintaining girlfriends, committing adultery, engaging in sexual relationships outside his covenant marriage, deceiving his wife, deceiving the congregation, or using spiritual authority to obtain romantic or sexual access to women under his influence, the biblical question is not merely whether he can still preach a powerful sermon.
The question is whether his life presently satisfies the character required of an overseer.
“Above reproach.”
“One-woman man.”
“Self-controlled.”
“Respectable.”
Managing his household faithfully.
Those words become difficult to reconcile with an ongoing pattern of deception and sexual unfaithfulness.
And if spiritual authority has been used to manipulate women, silence victims, demand secrecy, or protect the leader’s reputation, the situation becomes even more serious.
A shepherd is entrusted with sheep.
He is not given sheep to consume.
But perhaps you are reading this and thinking about someone specific.
Maybe the pastor was someone you trusted.
Maybe you defended him.
Maybe you ignored warning signs because his preaching moved you.
Maybe you were told:
“Touch not God’s anointed.”
Maybe questioning leadership was treated as rebellion against God.
Maybe you were pressured to protect “the ministry.”
Listen carefully.
Jesus does not need sin hidden in order to protect His name.
Christ is not honored when darkness is covered with religious vocabulary.
The church belongs to Jesus.
Not to the pastor.
Not to the founder.
Not to the denomination.
Not to the charismatic personality whose face appears on every poster.
Jesus Christ purchased His people with His blood.
That means protecting a reputation can never become more sacred than protecting Christ’s flock.
And perhaps the person reading this is not the wounded church member.
Perhaps it is the pastor.
Brother…
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe there is a second phone.
A conversation you keep deleting.
A woman whose name you changed in your contacts.
A relationship you keep calling “emotional support” because admitting what it has become terrifies you.
Maybe nothing physical has happened yet.
But you know why you hide the messages.
You know why your wife cannot see them.
You know why you would panic if they appeared on the projector Sunday morning.
You preach repentance while negotiating with your own secret.
And every Sunday the microphone gets heavier.
There is still time to stop running.
Not because exposure is impossible.
Because grace is still available.
Jesus did not shed His blood only for respectable sinners.
He died for adulterers.
Liars.
Hypocrites.
Sexually broken people.
Religious people.
Secret sinners.
Public sinners.
People who destroyed things they once promised God they would protect.
The cross does not tell us sexual sin is insignificant.
The cross tells us sin was so serious that Christ died—and grace is so astonishing that sinners who repent and believe can be forgiven.
That is the Gospel.
Not:
“Keep preaching until people forget.”
Not:
“Everybody makes mistakes.”
Not:
“God understands.”
Not:
“My calling excuses my conduct.”
The Gospel says:
Come into the light.
Confess.
Repent.
Stop manipulating.
Stop hiding.
Stop blaming your wife.
Stop blaming ministry pressure.
Stop blaming loneliness.
Stop using David’s failures to baptize your desires.
Stop using grace as camouflage.
Run to Christ.
There may be consequences.
There may need to be resignation.
There may need to be church discipline.
There may need to be professional counseling, accountability, disclosure to those legitimately affected, and years of rebuilding trust.

If coercion, abuse, exploitation, or criminal conduct is involved, church leaders should not treat the matter merely as an internal “spiritual problem”; appropriate safeguarding and civil authorities may also need to become involved.
Repentance is not controlling the consequences.
Repentance is surrendering the truth to God even when the truth costs you something.
And church, remember this:
The purpose is not humiliation.
The purpose is holiness.
The purpose is protection.
The purpose is repentance.
The purpose is restoration to Christ.
Because Christianity has never been the story of impressive people successfully hiding their scandals.
Christianity is the story of sinners meeting a Savior who refuses to leave them enslaved to what is destroying them.
Maybe that is why this question hurts so much.
Because somewhere underneath “Can a pastor have multiple wives and girlfriends?” is another question:
“Can someone fail terribly and still be loved by Jesus?”
Yes.
Absolutely yes.
But being loved by Jesus does not make rebellion holy.
Being forgiven does not make adultery permissible.
Being gifted does not make someone qualified.
Having thousands of followers does not overturn Scripture.
And having a powerful anointing story does not give anyone permission to build a private kingdom where biblical boundaries no longer apply.
Jesus forgave the woman caught in adultery, yet His mercy was never an endorsement of adultery.
Grace receives sinners.
Then grace begins changing them.
That is why our message at Gospel Warrior is not:
“From scandal to excuses.”
It is:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
He can rewrite the betrayed wife’s story.
He can rewrite the confused congregation’s story.
He can rewrite the wounded child’s story.
He can rewrite the woman who was manipulated by someone she trusted spiritually.
He can even rewrite the fallen pastor’s story.
But rewriting begins when we stop lying about the page we are currently on.
If this exposed something hidden in your own life, you do not need to announce every private detail publicly. But you do need to stop hiding from God and seek wise, trustworthy Christian help.
Let those words become more than engagement beneath an article.
Let them become the beginning of honesty.
It cannot.
Not because giving money proves you love Jesus.
It does not.
Christ cannot be bought.
But voluntary support can become one practical act of stewardship that helps Gospel-centered teaching continue reaching people who may never walk through the doors of a church.
If you want to support Gospel Warrior and go deeper with us:
And above everything else, glorify God by obeying Christ—whether or not you ever give Gospel Warrior a cent.
Because the greatest support you can give the Gospel is not your money.
It is a life surrendered to Jesus.
And when the scandals of men make you wonder whether Christianity is still worth believing, remember the line that darkness desperately wants you to forget:
Never measure the faithfulness of Jesus by the unfaithfulness of the person holding the microphone.
